utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Monday, April the 20th, 2009. I would like to greet the accused, as well as their counsels, as well as the representatives of the Office of the Prosecution, and all those assisting us in the courtroom. First of all, I would like to give the floor to the Registrar, who'd like to communicate an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 2D has submitted its list of documents to be tendered through Witness Korac, Davor. This list shall be given Exhibit IC987. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. The Chamber is going to make a -- going to render an oral decision proprio motu for the Stojic Defence. The Chamber recalls the decision of the guide-lines for the presentation of exculpatory evidence on 24 April 2008, and in particular paragraph 35 relating to guide-line 9. Any motion for the admission of documentary evidence must be submitted at the shortest possible moment after the presentation of all the evidence pertaining to a municipality or a given matter. The Chamber notes that to date the Stojic Defence has not filed any motion -- any written motion for the admission of evidence under guide-line 9. It could, therefore, infer that the Stojic Defence does not intend to file a motion under guide-line 9 on the matters for which it has finished its presentation. Indeed, the Chamber recalls that the Defence teams should not wait until the presentation of their case has ended to file such motions. This being said, the Chamber requests the Stojic Defence to file, before the 23rd of April, 2009, its observations on the absence of any motion filing under guide-line 9 at this stage. The Chamber also requests the Stojic Defence, also before the 23rd of April, 2009, to let it know of its intentions to file or not to file one or several motions under guide-line number 9, and if so, on which matters and under which timing. The Chamber wishes also to recall, for the benefit of the Stojic Defence, that the possible coming of Momcilo Mandic as a witness after the presentation of [indiscernible] will not, in any case, allow him to file a new request under guide-line 9 after he will have appeared, after this witness will have appeared. So, therefore, the Stojic Defence is invited to tell us, before the 23rd of April, what it intends to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. We gratitude, we accept this request, and we will meet it in the dead-line. We would just like to say that we did not submit that motion because the Defence was not introduced according to municipalities, but according to topics; and as we all know in the courtroom, the expert gave a framework, the one who was questioned first; and the witness today is a witness who will round off this one topic that has to do with the health topic; and we will submit our request and, by the 23rd, inform the Chamber what we intend to do and by when. And I acknowledge that if Witness Mandic is heard later, we will include the evidence for admission that refer to him. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Kovacic, you have two minutes because you requested two minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is okay. Your Honours, I would kindly ask me to permit an oral reply regarding the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, the interpreters cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We will try this one. I'm asking the Trial Chamber to permit me to give only one small item as reply to Prosecution's response to Slobodan Praljak's motion to add 253 exhibits to the Rule 65 ter. This response was submitted by the Prosecution on 16 April 2009. In the response, the Prosecution, inter alia, says that the Prosecution is prejudiced, as extremely few of those documents have been disclosed to the Prosecution. The problem is that all documents from the motion -- included in the motion were not released on the e-court. My reply to that is as follows: Due to the technical error, the Prosecution is right; all the documents were really not released. However, after this response, precisely during this weekend we find out this error, and now all the documents are released and all are available on the e-court. I hope that will assist the Prosecution to go into those documents and see what it's all about. I don't think this was necessary to file in written form, it would be sufficient, and it had to be replied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you fetch the witness, usher. Whilst we're waiting for the witness, we have a second oral decision which I'm going to read right away, a decision on the adding of several documents on the 65 ter motion of the Stojic Defence. The Stojic Defence has requested that nine exhibits should be added to its 65 ter list, to be submitted to the witness, Ivan Bagaric. The Petkovic Defence, on the 17th of April, 2009, pointed out it didn't oppose the request for the adding of 2D01540 on the 65 ter list submitted by the Stojic Defence. The other Defence teams and the Prosecution did not file any motion. First and foremost, the Chamber notes the withdrawal of the request for admission of 2D01535, submitted on April the 20th, 2009, and of the corrigendum submitted on the same day by the Stojic Defence on the latest motion filed on the 17th of April, 2009. The Chamber also notes or points out that the request for the adding of eight exhibits to the 65 ter list comes in very late because it was carried out only a few days before the appearance of Witness Ivan Bagaric. However, in spite of the late-coming of this request, the Chamber notes that the Stojic Defence could not obtain six out of the eight exhibits, i.e., Exhibits 2D01534, 2D01536, 2D01537, 2D01538, 2D01539 and 2D01540 at the moment. It only could get those documents at the moment of the proofing. Furthermore, the Chamber notes that these exhibits show some signs of reliability and probative value and relevance, and that the parties requested to present their observations did not invoke any harming of their interests because of the request coming in late, the request for the adding of exhibits. Therefore, the Chamber decides to admit the adding of those exhibits to the 65 ter list. However, for 2D00303 and for 3D00235, the Chamber points out that in its request of the 17th of April, 2009, the Stojic Defence pointed out that it already had those documents before the proofing of the witness, but that the need to submit them through Ivan Bagaric only appeared after the proofing of that witness. This explains why the adding to the list -- to the 65 ter list was made late --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Was requested late. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the Chamber's view that this is not a sufficient reason to justify such a late request for adding those exhibits to the 65 ter list. The explanation provided by the Stojic Defence in its corrigendum of the 20th of April do not justify the late submission of these exhibits; hence, the Chamber requests the -- the Chamber rejects the request for adding of 2D00303 and 2D00235.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you please stand. Could you please state your name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Ivan Bagaric, born on the 11th of November, 1961.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where do you work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right now, I am working at the Faculty of Medicine in Split and in Mostar, but I also am a deputy in the Assembly of the Republic of Croatia. This is my political duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. As a member of Parliament or a doctor, have you already been a witness before a court or is this the first time you have ever been a witness before a court, or is this the first time you have been a witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not the first time that I am testifying. I testified before in the case of Mr. Naletilic, but I testified to the general circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Naletilic case, were you a Prosecution or a Defence witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a witness for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Could you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. Doctor, since you have already testified, I'll keep it very brief, since you are familiar with the procedure. You will have to answer questions asked by Ms. Nozica, and she has prepared a series of documents which are in binders, which we'll receive when Ms. Nozica asks you questions on those documents. Please try and be accurate and brief in your answers. If there is a question you do not understand, even if it's a question asked by the Judges, do not hesitate to ask the one who asks you the question to rephrase it. You will first answer Ms. Nozica's questions, after which the other counsels of the other accused, as basically Ms. Nozica only represents Mr. Stojic, may ask you questions as well. The four Judges could also ask you questions to ask for clarification. After this, the Prosecutor, on your right-hand side, will cross-examine you and ask you questions as well. We have four days for your evidence. Since you're under oath, you're a court witness, which means that you're not to have any contact with Mr. Stojic's Defence and with anyone else on the content of your evidence. This is what I had to tell you. Without further adieu, I'd like to give the floor to Ms. Nozica, whom I'd like to greet again.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Once more, good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. Good afternoon, Mr. Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Before I begin with my examination, I would just like to say that Mr. Bagaric asked me, and I'm obliged to transmit this to the Court, we have planned four hours for the examination-in-chief of this witness; and we have made a calculation according to which the witness could complete his testimony by Thursday, within four days, in the courtroom this week; but the witness particularly asked, if possible, to stick to that because on Friday he needs to return in the afternoon to Zagreb because of the appointments he has there. So I would like to inform the Chamber about that right at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bagaric, I'm going to read or present to the Court briefly your particulars, and before we begin the examination, I would like you to confirm if all these particulars are correct. You are -- you graduated at the Faculty of Medicine in 1986 in Sarajevo. In 1986 until 1992, you worked as a doctor at the Tomislavgrad Medical Centre?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You were a deputy in the Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina after the first multi-party elections in the period from 1990 until 1998?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From March 1992 until September 1992, you were the chief of the main medical headquarters of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From September 1992 until 1996, you were first assistant head of the Defence Department and then assistant minister of defence for health in the HVO OZ-HB and then later in the Croatian section of the HZ-HB. You completed your specialisation from the topic of public health from 1995 to 1998?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From 1999 until 2001, you worked as assistant minister for health in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From 2001 until 2003, you worked at the Institute of Naval Medicine in Split?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From 2002 until today, you are a docent for public health at the Faculty of Medicine in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And in Split?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said today that you are a representative in the Assembly from 2003 until today, the Assembly of the Republic of Croatia, for Croatian citizens who live outside of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So if I understood that correctly, you represent all Croatian citizens in the Assembly of Croatia who happen to live outside the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, regardless of the fact if they live in Croatia -- in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Australia, Canada and so on. As long as they are Croatian citizens, I represent them in the Parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm going to deal with the period which we mentioned, it being that from March 1992, you were the chief of the main medical headquarters, and we're also going to deal with the period when you were the assistant head of the Health Department. Mr. Bagaric, we had a witness here who explained in some detail the forming of the HZ-HB Medical Corps, and I would like you now to do that as concisely and as briefly as possible, but your answer should discuss primarily your role in all of that, so how and when the Medical Corps of the HZ-HB was formed.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the question and the opportunity to speak here, Your Honours. I think that it is very important for everyone here to understand the context in which the Health Service of the HVO was organised, and it refers to the period mentioned by the counsel. After the open aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina and after overt aggression against the Republic of Croatia, excuse me, and evident preparations at the time of the Yugoslav Army and the Serbs, who rose against the Republic of Croatia, after the attack on the village of Ravno in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and all the preparations for war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, everything that was going on in the Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time in Sarajevo, we, especially us doctors who happened to be deputies as well, decided in a way to try to organise a kind of service which, in the event of war, would --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Bagaric. I would kindly ask you to slow down for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: We doctor, primarily those of us who were deputies in the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, decided to try and form a service that would respond to the needs of those who might need us, and who were those? Irrespective of whether they were civilians or soldiers, irrespective of their ethnic affiliation, at the beginning of 1992 we started to establish the Medical Service that later on would become the main Medical Corps, and later on it was integrated into the units of the Croatian Defence Council and, later on during the times of war, had to care for the wounded, unfortunately, both civilians and soldiers, and so on and so forth. How did we do that? To put it simply, we toured all of our settlements, the settlements with a major Croatian population, and by and large those with mixed population, because we were working together with Muslims, Bosniaks, and in those settlements we decided which points would be suitable to receive wounded, if that was the need, because there was an evident threat of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Primarily, we relied on our own civilian health institutions that existed there, and I'm talking about medical centres here. Besides having toured all those settlements, together with a specialist we also envisaged within the medical centres the so-called reception departments that receive wounded, if that was needed. What we did at the time we did together with Muslims and also with the Serbs who resided in the area. All of us together volunteered to establish a very serious preparation. Later on, when the military -- the so-called military units were already established at the municipal levels, we issued an order -- or, rather, we requested from the medical centres to appoint the so-called municipal medical heads that would somehow accompany the units which existed and were organised at the municipal level. Later on, when the brigades had already been formed after the HVO had been reorganised, we followed that reorganisation by assisting in logistics terms. We formed the Medical Service in the units of the Croatian Defence Council. I omitted to say that officially the so-called Main Medical Staff was established, and its tasks were the ones that I've already mentioned, and its task was also to be integrated and work by extending assistance to everybody, irrespective of whether they were civilians or soldiers. The only thing that we could rely on at the time was civilian medical service, i.e., medical centres. Later on, many of these medical centres, due to the circumstances of war, become the so-called war hospitals, and the war hospitals that we had established as such were also tasked with looking after the wounded. At a certain point in time, we lost communication with the large medical centres which before that both Muslims and Croatians used. That was before the war. Sarajevo was isolated, and a lot of specialists remained in the large medical institutions, and that's why we suffered a lack of doctors, equipment, and medical supplies. The Main Medical Staff was primarily tasked with providing logistical support or medical support to the points that I have already mentioned. Unfortunately, the conflict between Muslims and Croats which happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina resulted in the Croatian territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina hitting even harder times. You have to know that at one point in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croats were confined to several completely isolated enclaves in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, we will come to that. I apologise for interrupting. I just wanted to take things at a time. You have just now explained how the Medical Staff was established, the Main Medical Staff. Can you please tell me whether you were the head of that medical staff?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had the honour to serve as the head of the Main Medical Staff during the war, and later on, when the Defence Department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was established, it was integrated into the Defence Department. And later on, I assumed a different role. Actually, I was still the head of that Staff, but I was also appointed the assistant of the head of the Defence Department, and then when that Defence Department was reorganised and became a ministry, I became the assistant minister for defence within the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who and when appointed you as the assistant minister for health within the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I believe that I was appointed sometime in September, I believe, 1992. I was appointed by the Croatian Defence Council. Up to then, we already had an organised service on the ground which was then incorporated into the Croatian Defence Council, into its military part, that in a ceratin way defended the territories I've already spoken about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In a certain way, you've already answered and preempted my next question. My next question is: What was the task of the Health Department, and what were the principles of functioning within the Health Department? I would kindly ask you to tell us very briefly, what were your guiding principles?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Our task was to assist everybody and extend assistance to everybody who needed our help, and this is really what transpired. Everybody who needed help, irrespective of whether they were civilians or soldiers, irrespective of their ethnic background, they would receive our assistance. That was our main task. And as for our guiding principles that we -- that governed us, it was volunteerism. We could not order any one doctor to be engaged and to help us. It is well known that during the war, a lot of doctors, due to the war, had left the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and interestingly enough and very important would be to mention here, I compiled my Master's thesis on the subject of the organisation of the War Medical Service as a model; and I could then say that approximately 3.000 doctors had left the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and about 6700 medical technicians or other medical personnel had left. It was a major drain, and that's why we did not have a choice. We worked with those who were willing to work as volunteers, and our main principle was openness to everybody. We could not do anything else. We did not have a choice under the circumstances, faced with the situation. We had to develop the spirit of openness, and this was a good thing in all that misfortune, because our policy was based on accepting any expert [as interpreted], irrespective of their ethnic background. A very important and interesting characteristic of our service was the fact that irrespective of ethnic background, we extended help to people, and we also worked together, all of us, without regard to our ethnic background. For example, in Mostar during the war, we had two surgeons, and both -- we had actually several surgeons, not many, but two of them were Serbs. Throughout the entire war, they remained in Mostar and helped people. We had just one anesthesiologist, who was a Muslim. I don't want to go into great length. You can check that, and you can actually see what the meaning was of that openness, the common spirit, and fighting and struggle for every single patient.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, which services were part of the Health Department, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. I'm sure you will appreciate it, but let me try and remember. We had several re-organisations within the framework of our Medical Corps, and it all depended on the situation in the field. However, once we were integrated into the Defence Department of the HVO, then, within our own Health Department, we had the Main Medical Staff as the logistical part of the healthcare. Then we also had a department for looking after the wounded, and the third thing was the Control and Inspection Services, because our task was very important, not only when it came to the building up of the policies of the health system, but also its control and supervision, the control and supervision of its functioning. Later on, we were again reorganised as the situation demanded and as the need demanded at any given time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: You really must comply with the request to slow down, because it is impossible for the interpreters to follow you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before listening to you, Doctor, I have a technical question to ask you. If I understand you rightly, in the case of Mostar, a Croatian who was injured would be operated on by a Serbian surgeon, and the anesthetician [as interpreted] was a Muslim; that was the situation you described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It happened often, very often. However, Your Honour, this was a very common occurrence, but it did not happen all the time. I just provided that by way of an example and said that we had two Serb doctors and one anesthesiologist who was a Muslim. We also had other doctors. We had Croats and others, and they looked after the patients, irrespective of their national background. However, I need to mention the permanent lack of medical personnel. Save for the anesthesiologist whom I mentioned, we had to seek others, other persons who would be in charge of anesthesiology, and in addition to the surgeons that we had, their numbers were never sufficient. We had to seek others, and we managed to make due in order to make the system work. However, we were all the time faced with a lack of personnel and a lack of equipment. That was our biggest problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, I know that you are a temperamental person and it is a problem for you to speak slowly. However, we will need to slow down, and we will need to make short breaks between my question and your answer. You just explained which services existed within the Health Department. Could you please tell the Trial Chamber who the heads of these services were subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Since I was the head of the organisation of health in the Croatian Defence Council, heads of particular departments, as we called them, were subordinated directly to me. In a certain way, I was their commander, as it were, although we were primarily colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, we're talking about things in general, and you told us already, but let me ask you again. You said that throughout all that time in the territory of the HZ-HB, there was a lack of medical personnel, doctors and all the other medical personnel. Could you please provide us with a general assessment as to whether the Health Service of the HZ-HB had at its disposal enough medical supplies and equipment, including drugs and medicines?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: All that time, we were faced with a major and terrible lack of everything. There was a scarcity of everything. There was a lack of medicines, equipment, and people; and this especially applied to the areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was inhabited by Croats, who were completely isolated from the rest of the state, like, for example, the hospital in Nova Bila, Zepce, Kiseljak, and so on and so forth. For example, in Orasje, the situation was bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It transpires from your answers that you were the assistant of the Defence Department in the Health Sector -- I apologise, in the Defence Department. What I would like to know is this: Could you tell us whether, in the Defence Department, you had meetings of the collegium, and how often did they take place, if they did?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: We doctors maintained frequent contacts. We worked together in our medical staffs. However, when it comes to the Defence Department, I would like to say that, yes, we did have meetings of the collegium. I can't tell you exactly how often they took place. It was every now and then. Sometimes it would happen every week, sometimes once in a fortnight, but I believe that it was done every time a need arose.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber how decisions were made at the collegium, at least at those meetings that you attended and of which you have direct experience?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all the microphones that are not needed be switched off, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the nature of the work that I carried out, and practically constantly being out in the field, going here and there, I was perhaps not able to attend every single collegium meeting. I did attend them, but not every single one. And when I attended them, the characteristic was a discussion about problems in the way certain positions were adopted, and if any of the assistants had some proposals, they were discussed. And, in a way, after the discussion, certain conclusions were adopted.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, you, as an assistant in the Health Sector, as part of the Defence Department, how independent were you in decision-making in decisions that pertain to your field of expertise?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, since I am a doctor and because, in a way, we already had a pretty structured health service set up already, to a large degree I would say, well, I don't remember having any problems in communication, or in being independent, or in the implementation of the things that I was in charge of, so I had a high degree of freedom or autonomy and independence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that everything that is happening around you in the courtroom can maybe distract you, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I just have a question, something specific to ask from the witness. Witness, you were an assistant in the Department of the Defence or the Defence Department, in charge of health matters. At the same time, was there also a chief of the Health Department within the HVO, and what were your -- what was your relationship with him? Because you speak of your independence and so on, so I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is an excellent question, and I'm glad that you have put it. At the civilian level, there was a chief of the head -- of the Health Service, and later he was the minister of the Health Service, and that is my dear colleague Mr. Ivan Sarac. When we're talking about autonomy of my work, what I mean is the part that has to do with hospitals, with the structuring of the service in the military units of the HVO, and he was in charge of that part that did not belong to that. These were civilian institutions, such as health sectors which were not part of that sector. But we did coordinate our work constantly because everything that we had in the HVO units was something that we were borrowing from the civilian health sector, so that is that so-called integral structure of the Health Service, and it's known in the world of health organisation. It's something that is described as a model of organising the work of the Health Sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, I am going to ask you to explain, if you can, this degree of autonomy that you had in decision-making. When you attended the collegiums and when you discussed other areas, and when other assistants, assistants from the Defence Department of Mr. Stojic also attended, were you able to draw any conclusions about their autonomy and proposing and decision-making? Did you have any position on that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I think that I did not mention the fact that this level of autonomy that I had to a certain degree, and the kind of professional relationship that I had with the chief of the sector, was something that others had too. I don't know what the relationship of each individual assistant was. It's something that I cannot know. But on the basis of what I saw, and based on my attendance and what I was able to see at the collegium meetings, the relationship of others also was professional.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, you also touched upon this topic. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber how the Health Service was organised in the HVO HZ-HB units? What I'm primarily thinking of here -- well, you said that first they were municipal HVO units and then the brigades began to be structured. So from that time-period on, what was the health organisation like in the units?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: When you say "units," what I mean are military units, the military component of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council. So as an HQ body, in a way, in a professional sense, we coordinated the work and, in a way, were setting up that structure, as such; and it was set up in such a way that each, let's say, squad had its own trained medic, each company had a higher-trained medical technician, and that every brigade had its own doctor. The brigade also had its own doctor. And what is important to say is also that, in a way, we were implementing a policy of the highest possible degree of autonomy of the Health Corps within the HVO. And then, as opposed to the previous Yugoslav model, we tried, wherever this was possible, to extract the Health Sector from the Logistics Sector, as such. In some places, we were successful; in others, we were not. This depended on the commander of the unit. The goal was that those doctors were given the status of assistants so that they could be as independent as possible in their work and medical care. I mean, I could speak a lot more about that topic, but I think that that is enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, I wish we could have as much time as we wanted on each topic so that you could explain as much as you wished, but unfortunately our time is limited, so sometimes I would have to stop you, even though that sometimes can be to my detriment. So in any case, can you please tell me, when you said that there were people in charge of the health assignments in the units, who were they subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I think that I answered that question already. At the level of the military regions, we had the health chief, so he had the status of the commander of the military sector. Then we had the assistant, who was the assistant of the brigade commander. So in the hierarchy, when we're talking about the military structure, they were an integral part of a certain formation and they were directly responsible to the commander. When we're talking about this professional aspect, for example, when we're talking about some specific circumstances, for example, the implementation of preventive health, then from the Administration Health Service or the Medical Corps HQ, we could issue instructions. I would even write orders, because I didn't know how to communicate in other ways. But, anyway, this was something that we used in order to communicate professionally amongst each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could look at a few documents now. If the witness does not have with you documents -- the document binder, perhaps the usher could give you those documents, but in any case could you please look at the first binder of documents and now let's look at this topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at the first document, 2D567. It's a decision on the internal organisation of the Defence Department of the 17th of October.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I would need some help here. 2D --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That should be the first document. If you have the first binder, it's after this list. I think you have the documents marked with stickers at the side.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, thank you very much. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So it's a decision about the internal organisation of the Defence Department, adopted by Bruno Stojic, and approved by Mr. Boban on the 10th of November, 1992. Could you please look at item 5 pursuant to this decision in order to see how matters from the Health Sector were resolved, and it says in the chief for -- in the health section -- could the interpreters please look at the original on e-court. "In the Medical Sector, chief of the Medical Care for the Wounded, chief of the Medical Staff, chief of the Medical Brigade Corps, chief of the Control Inspections Service and directors of war hospitals are appointed by the head of the Defence Department at the proposal of the assistant head for the Medical Services." Mr. Bagaric, according to this decision more or less from the month of September, when you were appointed assistant chief, did you propose -- and I'm going to only limit it to the chief of the brigade Medical Corps referred to here. Can you recall how and in which way were these people appointed to the position of chief of the brigade medical corps?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Things were as you have just read out. However, before we joined the Defence Department, in a certain way at the municipal level, and I'm talking about the Main Medical Corps, we appointed people, and this was more a matter of agreement as to who that would be. When it came to the establishment of the brigades, within the brigades the commander or the medical service that he relied on - I'm talking about doctors in the medical centres - in a certain way they were the ones who selected, who agreed as to who would be what in the unit. By and large, but not always, but very often this would be done at that proposal of the brigade commander. I did not see a problem there, and there were no problems with the functioning at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we proposed somebody somewhere, I cannot remember, although this also applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, 2D702. This is a decision of your appointment on the 8th of September, 1992, and this accords with your recollection of what happened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, 2D1352, please. I would like you to look at page 2D660126. I'm just waiting for it to appear on e-court. And if you can look at the list, this is the Health Sector and this is the salary list for November 1992. There is a list here of persons, and perhaps you can tell me about how many persons worked in the Health Sector from September, when you were appointed assistant chief, until the end of, let's say, 1993. What were the approximate numbers in the service?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not that important. I think that this is the first salary that was received. Before that, there were no salaries issued. But in any case, this number varied because of the requirements, but also because of that element of the volunteers. Simply, somebody who was available could have left for their own personal reasons to do something else or to leave their job in the army, so the number ranged from 25 to 30 people, all in all, and they were directly subordinated to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we look at 2D752. This is a diagram of the Health Sector, and for the purpose of the transcript I would like to say this is document 2D, that is the decision on internal structuring, 2D567; in paragraph 13, it states that the diagram is an integral part of the decision. So I would just like to you comment on the diagram and explain, once again, this relationship of subordination, who was subordinated to you, and how can that be clarified with the help of this diagram.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, it's very simple. It's clearly indicated here, in a way. So the Health or the Medical Sector had three entities that were a part of it. That was the Healthcare Sector, the Inspection Unit and the Medical Corps HQ, which was the Medical/Logistical Sector. The other two were operational sectors that had jobs in the field and were touring and so on. The chiefs of these sections were directly subordinated to me, and in their work, as can be seen here, in a way relies on the healthcare for the wounded. They are in charge of the surgical staff, the medics, the trained medical personnel that was in lower units. So, in a way, that was the professional chain that was part of the structure of the Medical Corps of the HVO. What is important to mention here, and I didn't mention it before, and I apologise to the Trial Chamber, is the following: The war hospitals that we had, about 20, also had a very high degree of autonomy and, in a way, they relied on our medical care service. They were suffering from a shortage of doctors, of medical equipment and so on, so they provided support to us and we provided support to them. So the Medical Corps had several sections. One of them was the Donor Sector, so it was a unit that was in charge of gathering funds either from international organisations or from individuals or international organisations. Their job was to collect enough equipment and medicines in order for us to be able to work. So this is more or less the structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, I would just like to mention, since we're looking at the diagram, part of the Medical Corps HQ. Later, we're going to discuss the more detailed work of this service, but we had the epidemiological/toxicological service, so can you tell us what the primary task of this service was?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: This service was perhaps the most important service, in addition to the hospitals and the healthcare for the wounded, so this would have been the most important service within the Medical Staff. Its role was to look after the hygiene and the epidemiology situation about prophylaxis and anti-epidemics measures. In the entire area where our units existed and irrespective of the type of the institution, wherever we thought that an infection could break out and epidemics could break out, and whenever and wherever it was necessary to carry out constant surveillance and control. In addition to that, this service was in charge of the ongoing education, because we know, when we're talking about the units of the Croatian Defence Council, that those were people who had never been in the army, or just a few of them were. And when we're talking about a medical staff we have to know that those people knew virtually nothing or very little about war or military healthcare, so at the same time we had to educate all of our staff to bring them up to a high standard. I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, I would like us to look at the next three documents. Let us just locate the things that you have talked about, and let's see what establishment positions are we talking about within the units when it comes to the Medical Corps. Could you please look at 2D927. That's our next document. This is the prescribed establishment of the command of the operation zone which was signed by Mr. Stojic. When we're talking about the operation zone, could you look at position number 30, which should be on page 4 or the penultimate page, both in English and in Croatia. It says at the top "The chief of the Medical Service," and then it does that say "chief," but it does say "Medical Service." Would that be the person that was a member of the operation zone by establishment?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's now look at 2D1370. That's our next document. This is a diagram of the establishment of the brigade. On page 4 in the Croatian version and on page 6 in the English version, under item number 8, could you please take a look at what it says there. It says: "The chief of the Medical Service"; would that be correct? This is page 4 or the penultimate page.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So this is the position in the establishment of the brigade, that would be the person in charge of the Medical Service?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at another document. P566 is the number, and that's another diagram, the diagram of the establishment of a battalion, in both Croatian and English diagrams -- versions, the diagram is on page 2, and under the Logistics Platoon to the very right, it says the "Logistics Platoon," it says "Technical Department" and it also says "Medical Department," and "Quarter-master's Department." Can we agree that we're talking about a department that existed in --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise, that's how it should have been. However, due to the lack of personnel and staff, as a rule the positions were not filled, at least not -- they were not filled to the extent that they should have been filled, due to the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, I'm now going to ask you to look at the following document, which is 2D01540 [Realtime transcript read in error, "2D540"] this should be the following document in your binder.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. This is a document that you gave me during your proofing session. It had been sent to you by Mr. Bruno Stojic, where it says because of the problems with the command and control of the units of the HVO, when it comes to the war healthcare, and in order to resolve the situation which arose as a result of the lack of respect for military organisation "I hereby issue the following order." Could you please explain, how does the order deal with the issue of subordination and the chain of command? And this in military terms, could you please comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a correction to the transcript. On page 9, line 17, the document number is indicated as 2D540, and I have the feeling it is 2D01540.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You are absolutely right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: 2D01540, I suppose that we all have it and see it. It was just an error in the transcript. I'll bear that in mind. Go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I assume that this order was drafted at my own proposal. I can't be sure of that, but I assume. And the reason was the lack of respect in the field of all the things that I've already spoken about. So this is just an explanation and an instruction as to how to proceed. And in a certain way, this confirms what I have just been talking about, and that is that the doctors, at unit levels, were responsible for the healthcare, and their position was that of the assistant chief of the unit, and this is very important for the autonomy and for the most efficient work of the service. It was important for them to have a direct link with the commander, and they were also reporting to the commander of the unit for everything that had to be done in line with the actions of the unit. I repeat, when it comes to the professional part, they were also connected with us, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at item 6, where it says that the chief of the war healthcare of the operations zone for the functioning of wartime healthcare in the operations zone, and in professional sense, he submits reports and is responsible to the Ministry of Defence Sector for Healthcare.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is precisely what I've told you, and in professional terms, he was responsible to the person that we saw in the diagram, the person who was in charge of the service for the healthcare for the wounded in the Healthcare Sector. That's the link.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now when we're talking about the problems of functioning and the chain of command, this is something that we will discuss at a later stage. However, we will keep in mind your answer, where you said that there were problems in the field from time to time. Can we now look at the last document, which is P6379 -- P06379 is the number of the document, the last one in the series about the topic I wanted to introduce to the Tribunal, and show the Tribunal what positions you held and what you did, and that's why I'm showing you the decision on the appointment of the commission for investing war crimes in the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and here you can see your own name. Under number 6, the commission was set up on the 3rd of November, 1993. Mr. Bagaric, did you know that you had been appointed, and did you participate in the work of this commission?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: This is a document that I never saw before, and I don't know whether I was appointed, and the commission never became operational, and I'm not excluding that or maybe instead of me there was somebody else, a colleague of mine who bore the same name and a different family name, which is something that the honourable Judge asked me about, and he was in charge of civilian healthcare. That may also be the case, because I never saw this document before and I never personally participated in the work of this commission.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This will suffice. Thank you very much. Mr. Bagaric, within the framework of the Healthcare Sector in the Defence Department, and I'm talking primarily about you, did you submit certain reports? And later on we will see whether anybody reported to you. Did you submit certain reports, who did you report to, and how often? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Of course, of course I submitted written reports. I provided certain documents. I drafted certain documents, and those documents were actually prepared by my colleagues who were in charge of certain activities, and those were our reports which we would, from time to time, send to the Defence Department which was later on the Ministry of Defence. However, I also remember that we often sent reports to other addressees as well, to some international organisations, to some institutions who expected information from us in order for them to be able to act and help us, and this is what we did. I can't remember, but I repeat that this was not a regular occurrence, it never happened every seven or every fifteen days. It was more or less twice a month, sometimes even once a month, but I believe that it depended on the situation and on the need at hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you to look at certain documents that speak about that. The first one would be 2D721, which should be the next one in your binder.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a report for January 1993, but there is no precise date. Could you please confirm? I can't say whether this is your signature or not. You can confirm that for us, and would you say that this is the type of report that you possibly submitted to various addressees?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I must admit that this report is not typical of our work. It lacks some numbers and everything else that a heading should contain. However, I do not doubt the correctness and the accuracy of this report, because I can see who signed it. I'm familiar with the signature, although the majority of these documents that were sent from our Healthcare Sector, my name was already indicated as the commander. But I spoke about the high level of collegial relationship, and I trusted my men, and they did not have to wait for my signature to be put on the document. They could sign it themselves. Very often, they would. That would follow telephone consultations if I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at the following document, which is 2D739.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may quickly ask a question regarding the previous document. I don't know whether something escaped me, but can you explain the abbreviation "HE"? "Extremely poor HE situation, HE team."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you for your question, Your Honour. This is Hygiene and Epidemiology Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You've looked at document 2D739. Again, this is your signature, but it was signed on your behalf. Just briefly tell us -- you already started telling us that people --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a more typical report, although it is very short. However, this is the kind of document that we sent. This is actually a report for a certain period of time. This one is from the 13th of July, 1993, to 2nd August 1993, the report on the functioning of the Healthcare Sector. This could be one of the more regular reports, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at the following document. I'm just showing you the reports that the Defence has been able to locate. I don't know whether they're yours or not, and I don't know that there were more of them. The next one is 2D738. That's the next report that we have been able to locate among the documents.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: This is my signature, and this is it, yes. This is a report that I sent.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And can we have another, which is 2D714. The period is 7 September to 13 September 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Mr. Bagaric, on behalf of the Healthcare Sector did you compile reports that could be half annual, annual, and did you send such reports to the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now can we look at P00128. This is our next document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: My apologies. Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: P00128. This should be the next document in your binder after the previous one, after the one that you are now looking at.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, you have it in the electronic courtroom, so maybe you can rely on that. I am sure that you will find it easier. Can we now look at page 14 in the Croatian language, which is also page 13 in the English language. At the beginning, you saw the front page and the title, the report on the work --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I can't follow you. I don't have the document and I can't follow you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You don't have it in the binder?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: No, I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we ask the assistance of the usher? Can you please assist the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you repeat the number?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P after the document that you have just looked at, P00128.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 0018 -- oh, sorry, yes, I've got it. I'm sorry, I apologise. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So this is a report on the work of the HZ-HB for 1992. It's a collective report, and you have noticed yourself that it says "Mostar, March 1992," which is an obvious error because this is a report that was compiled in March 1993. Page 4 in the Croatian and page 13 in the English versions speak about healthcare. It says here, and I'm just going to read or underline some things that you've already spoken about. You said: "In the month of February 1992, we started working on the establish of the Healthcare service. On the 8th of March, 1992, we established the Main Medical Staff headquartered in Tomislavgrad." I am going to ask you to look at the last paragraph, which is the part that you've already spoken about. Can you please skip a few paragraphs here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, because it took me some time to check something. Witness, I'd like to come back to the previous document, which is a report for the time-frame. It is document 2D714. It is a report dated September the 13th -- the 7th. A detail struck me. It seems that General Praljak is doing something for one of these sons of Mr. Silajdzic. This Haris Silajdzic, was he a Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I don't see in the text what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I can help the witness in the Croatian text. The previous document, 2D714, third paragraph, please, third paragraph on the first page on the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Silajdzic has leukemia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that has nothing to do with Silajdzic, because this is Haris Silajdzia [phoen]. Your Honour, it's a typical situation where, in a way, an intervention was required, and this was often done in order to help a child that needed help. I think that that has nothing to do with Silajdzic. The last name here is Silajdzia. It's a different last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you sure? Fine, I was just checking. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I think, yes. I assume that they are not related.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe that Mr. Praljak will talk about that, too. We had an opportunity, actually, to see another document that pertains to this evacuation. I think we already looked at it in the courtroom, so I am coming back to the report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can just say one thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This talks about what I was saying earlier, that the situation in our hospitals was quite serious, and in Rama -- it's a village, we didn't have a hospital there, so Mr. Praljak here intervened quite honorably, because a child cannot be treated in that hospital because it's suffering from leukemia; so this is evidence of what I mentioned before about the problems that we were encountering.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Doctor, I know you have very sensitive about this question that I'm going to put to you right now unfortunately; well, I understand you completely, but I must put the question. This child just happened to be of Bosnian ethnicity, and we can affirm that based on first and last name. I know this is something that makes you angry, because you talk about the actions of medical workers and their principals, who should not pay any attention to that, but I need to ask you about this in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, I wondered about this, because if in the war we did not pay attention to who was what, we worked together and we treated everyone, then it seems senseless to pay attention to something like that. But I assume that a child with a name such as Haris Silajdzia is a child of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: There will be more questions like this, but you must understand that the name and the indication of ethnicity according to the name is something that is not clear to everyone in the courtroom in the same way that it is clear to you. So let us now look at 0128. I indicated on page 14, I said this was actually page 13 in the English, and the last paragraph begins -- we're already on page 14 in the English, and it's the passage before last of the section that refers to the health, and it says: "By forming of the Defence Department of the HZ-HB, the General Medical Staff, together with the Service for the Welfare of the Wounded and the Control and Inspection Service, to form our Health Sector." Mr. Bagaric, this is actually what you talked about, about the functioning of the Main Medical Corps headquarters, and that it was part of the Medical or the Health Sector?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Can you tell me what page it is?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's page 14 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I don't see page 14. Ah, no, no, excuse me, excuse me. I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The last paragraph, Mr. Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, actually, that confirms what I said before, with the formation of the Defence Department and the Main General Medical Corps, united with the Service for the Welfare of the Wounded and the Control and Inspection Service, form the Health Sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The evacuation of wounded and civilians from besieged towns, for example, Jajce was organised, was that one of the important actions of the Health Sector at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was very important, very important. This was a time when the Muslims and Croats from Bosnia defended with full faith the territory and were all together part of the HVO. We're talking about Jajce, but because of the Serb strength, we had to leave the town. And previously these doctors, whom I am proud of and who I mentioned before, the ones who were at the head of these services, personally, in personnel carriers or, rather, in buses; so in improvised transportation that happened to be armoured, pulled out all the wounded from Jajce, including all the Muslims and the Croats, before the fall of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, we're going to return to this topic a bit later, but now, since it is the time for the break, I would just like to ask you about a piece of information that is significant. Can you tell me when this is happening, the period you're talking about, the fall of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, I have a problem really with numbers, with time. This is something that is quite condensed to me, this wartime period. I think this was in late 1992, so it was probably September or October when Jajce fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bagaric. Your Honours, can we now go on a break and then before we move on to our next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before we resume, Mr. Witness, the Chamber would like you to answer perhaps at a slower pace, because the interpreters have problems. We know that you are a very good speaker, but please try and control the speed of your delivery.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, I'm going to ask you -- well, earlier we saw a report for the first six months of 1992. Can you look at document P4699. That should be the next document in your binder. It's a report of the HVO about the work for the period from January to June 1993. I'm going to ask you -- yes, 1993 -- to look at page 29 in the Croatian, and that is page 19 in the English, and just tell me when you've found it.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is where the report begins its section on the Health Service. I'm going to go to page 30. It's a large report. Everyone can look. I'm going to focus on the third paragraph on page 30, and that is the last paragraph on page 19 in the English, and it says: "At the moment, the greatest problem is the means of transport, primarily off-road vehicles, medical vehicles, which are practically nonexistent but which are essential for the transport of the wounded." And then it says this problem is particularly evident in the Northern Herzegovina and Central Bosnia sectors, and then it goes on to talk about the lack of professional medical staff. In terms of the means of transport, you emphasised this here as one of the problems in your report, it is one of the problems that is mentioned first, can you please tell Their Honours what the situation was in terms of the transport vehicles?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, this primarily refers to vehicles -- emergency medical vehicles, ambulances, which were meant for the units in the field to transport the wounded from inaccessible terrain, and that is why it says here explicitly that these are all-terrain vehicles. But generally there was a constant shortage of vehicles for the transport and care of our wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we now look at page 31, paragraph 2, and in the English that is paragraph 4 on page 20. It talks about the Epidemiological and Toxicological Service, which you said was part of the Main Medical Corps HQ, and there is a sentence in the middle of the paragraph which says that the main task of this service is the prevention of infectious diseases in the -- in units of the armed forces of the HZ-HB. The training programme included the following: medical inspection of the water supply; medical inspection of food; inspection of military accommodation, both in barracks and at the front; medical inspection of refugees and displaced persons, with the aim of preventing the spread of contagious diseases amongst the armed forces of the HZ-HB; the disposal of waste, both in barracks and at the front. And it goes on to say tetanus vaccination, implementation of DDD measures, active search for infected patients and those with signs of infection, a military and medical approach, and a unique wartime medical doctrine in the approach to infectious diseases. Mr. Bagaric, does this actually represent a description of the assignments of the Infectious, Epidemiological and Toxicological Service?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a preventive medical healthcare sector, and there is an important sentence in the continuation of the text. The important aspect of this matter is that: "Besides oral instructions during medical inspections of troops before their departure for the front, heads of medical brigades were given adequate instructions by this service."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now to look at another report, and this is a report for the second half of 1993, from July to December. This is P7419. What I would like to ask you about is actually on page 2. No, I'm sorry, I apologise, the Health Sector actually is dealt with on page 6. I would like to draw your attention to a detail from this report. In the English, this is on page 3, the fifth sentence from the bottom, where it says: "One of the most serious problems in wartime medical care," and that's the abbreviation "RZ, Ratno Strasno [phoen]," am I correct, "is a shortage of personnel. A considerable number of medical staff left the HR-HB at the beginning of the war and mostly got jobs in the Republic of Croatia. Even though the main Medical Corps headquarters did their utmost to have them return, they were not very successful in that." Mr. Bagaric, is what is written in this report for the July/December 1993 period something that could have applied to the entire wartime period?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, a very brief clarification first. In 1992, we were joining the service or the Medical Corps on a volunteer basis exclusively, but in time, as the war went on, more and more people were leaving, dropping out, and they were leaving primarily for Croatia; so we really did everything that we could, in talking to them, trying to persuade them, to explain to those who left, but we were not successful in keeping most of these cadres. And this is something that does apply throughout the whole wartime period, both for Croats and for Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we look at another document on this topic, and this is 2D1536. It's the next document in your binder. It is an order by Mr. Boban where, as we can see, it says on the 3rd of June, 1992. Actually, we were dealing with a report for the end of 1993, and now we are returning to the 3rd of June, 1992, where an order is issued to the municipal staffs of the HVO, where it says: "All medical personnel, except those in the Grude Hospital who worked in Mostar, must immediately return to their posts. All of those who do not follow this command must be fired immediately and criminal charges must be brought against them." Mr. Bagaric, we can see from this that at least from June 1992 until the end of 1993, this was a prominent problem, at least pursuant to this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but this is a particular situation here. We're talking about Mostar. At the time, I was not in Mostar, and at the request of probably one of the commanders of the Mostar Hospital, the order on this was signed so that people should return to Mostar from neighbouring towns in order to be able to provide medical services.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now we're moving briefly to another topic which does deserve more time, but I'm going to ask you to actually just go through it briefly. Mr. Bagaric, can you please tell me whether the Health Sector conducted training in the application of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: As part of the preventive medical work, on one hand, and, on the other hand, the section that was called the Sector for Information and Investigation or Research, sent out these brochures that talk about first aid and also instructs about the implementation or application of international humanitarian law. I saw quite frequently that this was used by the commanders as well, the most responsible people who were at the head of the HVO, because I did see a few commands to that effect, a few orders to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us now look at 2D751. That would be the next document after this one. This is a -- is this the brochure that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely that one, or perhaps it was a similar one. There were others, similar ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we have a clean transcript? You're saying it's this brochure or similar brochures? You need to wait for my question to be recorded first. So this particular brochure or similar ones were distributed to members in the Health Sector who were providing medical services; did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document. This is P2050. It's an order signed by Mr. Stojic and Mr. Petkovic of the 24th of April, and it states that there is a need, while providing medical health, to ensure that at all times your doctors and medical workers' approach to any wounded, regardless of whether it's a civilian or a member of the enemy formations, all civilians and all commanders should be treated exclusively pursuant to international conventions and regulations. This was sent to the commanders of operational zones and all other commanders. You said you had the opportunity to see in the field that certain commanders also issued orders like this. Did you also mean this kind of order as well?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely what I was thinking of. This is one of that kind of order.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, now I'm going to ask you to be as brief as possible, to be as efficient as possible. I'm not going to say faster, at the expense of quality, but we are going to talk about a topic that concerns reports that were arriving from the field. Let me ask you, first, did you receive reports about the state of the Medical Corps in the HZ-HB? I emphasised that already when we were looking at your monthly reports and saw some summary results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, I would like to ask you to -- just for a minute to say the following: that on line, I believe - what was it - 11, line 11, "all civilians and all commanders should be treated exclusively pursuant to international conventions and regulations," I believe in this case it is not commanders but all civilians and combatants. It is what you might have said. So instead of "commanders" here, it should be "combatants," in accordance with the language of the relevant international conventions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may complement. In the document, actually it is civilians and prisoners, but I could not recall what you have said exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was reading from the document, which is P2050. In the second paragraph, it says: "According to civilians and prisoners," so these are the two categories. This is exactly what the document says. Very well. Thank you very much for your intervention.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Bagaric, we're coming back to the topic of reports that you may have observed about the situation with the medical care in the territory of the HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did receive reports more or less often which depended on the area from which they came, and it depended on the situation, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm now going to show you a certain number of reports, but before that, could you please a summary assessment of those reports? Can you please tell us what they contain? Was there a template? Did the reports follow the template, or whether they were sometimes totally off the template, if it existed? I apologise, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: At first, that was done as needed, without any templates to follow. However, later on there was, indeed, a template introduced, and that template was respected, in a sense. However, there was a long period of time when we received reports about our dead and wounded; the names, the family names, where they were wounded, when they died.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And all those reports and summaries, did they result in summary reports which provided a total number of wounded and dead?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I know that because of the lack of any regular communication with every unit, we certainly did not manage to compile comprehensive reports. However, that was done and finally reproduced summary reports in order to be able to follow the situation on the ground and plan the Healthcare Service accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we now please look at 2D00222, which should be the following document in your binder. This document or, rather, these documents that I'm going to show you follow a chronological order which will help us see what was happening during that period of time, and in this particular report the HVO Brigade Eugen Kvaternik from Bugojno, on the 26th of January, 1993, provides a list of wounded combatants in the territory of Bugojno from 24 January 1993. Later on, we will see what happened -- what later happened in Bugojno. And now can we just look at the list from 1 through 20, and you will see the names of that particular brigade which were of Croatian and Muslim origins. If you look at the names, can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that a large number of those people were Muslims, Bosniaks, and still members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we now look at 2D98, which should be the next document in your binder. This document was sent from Vitez. The date is 19th of April. It was signed by Mr. Drago Dzambas, the chief of the Medical Service of the Operational Zone Central Bosnia; wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
