utterances.text: And it is a report that we will dwell upon for a little while, and it says here: "From April 17 (from 1100 hours) until today, April 19th, the situation in the territory of Central Bosnia has been rapidly deteriorating." In the first part, reference is made to the attacks on the BiH Army in the municipalities of Vitez, Zen [phoen], Busovaca, in the places called Kakanj, Konjic, Fojnica, and I repeat, Kakanj, Konjic, Fojnica, and also Zenica, Kiseljak and Kresevo, and the following paragraph says: "At the triage war hospital in Nova Bila (Franciscan Hospital) from the beginning until today, there have been 100 wounded of whom three people died at the hospital. The number of fallen combatants and civilians in the territory of Central Bosnia ranges from 60 to 65 altogether." And the following paragraph, I'm reading from the second sentence, it says: "We are especially asking you to protest with the UNPROFOR, because they transport Muslim soldiers to Travnik, they transport medicines and medical supplies to them, and we, on the other hand, are unable transport our own wounded to the hospital." Later on, we will go back to the hospital in Nova Bila and talk about that, but at the moment could you please explain to the Trial Chamber under what conditions the hospital operated, and could you please say something about the objection of the chief of the Medical Corps of Central Bosnia about the unequal treatment extended by UNPROFOR to the Croatian wounded, on the one hand, and the Muslim wounded, on the other?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: First of all, both -- the hospital in Nova Bila was a hospital that existed in a very typical war environment. It was housed in a Franciscan church. The patients who would be brought there were put on church benches that were used as beds. Very few people provided surgical services with very obsolete equipment, unfortunately. This report here that we're looking at primarily concerns the problem with the organisation of the service and caring for the wounded under such circumstances, and I would say that this person is not requesting but imploring somebody to help. Who is he imploring with? Everybody. We were just one of the addressees. Before that, he must have spoken to the international organisations and he must have addressed them as well. In this particular case, I can't say whether my colleague, Dzambas, was right when he said that UNPROFOR provided unequal help and treated the Croatian side unfairly. However, I can speak from my own experience and say that during the war, the international organisations disappointed me. I had expected a more powerful response, without any strings attached. However, very often, when I personally asked for their help and assistance, they always wanted to strike a balance, they always wanted to see whether the other side received the same, and that's why the help was very often late, particularly from the International Red Cross and other international organisations. Still, one has to say that we have to be very grateful and recognise those people who came to help us under such dire circumstances. Without them, the situation would have been even worse, because from them we could only receive help.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When we're talking about a hospital in Bila, could you please tell us what the situation was like? We see that the situation was like that on the 19th of April, 1993, but can you tell us for how long the hospital existed and for how long it operated under such circumstances existing in an enclave without any possibility of anybody else accessing them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: It was a very sad story which lasted from approximately this time to the moment when the Washington Peace Accords were signed, and that was, I believe, in 1994, in the month of March. Throughout all that time, the hospital in Nova Bila was completely blocked and encircled. They could not receive any assistance. They could not transport their wounded anywhere. They could only be air-lifted. That was the only way for the wounded to be transported.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We will -- I would like us to proceed. We'll go back to the hospital. I know that hospital is very important, and it was a very important topic of your contacts with international organisations. We will come back to that and talk about it a bit further. Can we please now look at 2D779. That's the next document in your binder. This is another report which was signed by Zrinko Brekalo Dr. Zrinko Brekalo and he's requesting certain drugs and medicines, and then he provides a list of the civilians who were killed in Trusina on the 16th of April. You know Mr. Brekalo, don't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is that one of the ways how you received information from the field?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a story about Konjic, i.e., about Kostajnica. And just for the transcript, I would like to say this document has two pages. The first one is 2D52 -- and the second 52 -- 2D520240, and the second page is 2D520241. And the second page does not belong to the document, actually. The ERN number of the document which we took from the Prosecutor, and the ERN numbers are in sequence, but the second page does not belong to the documents. So when we tender this document for admission, we will ask for the admission of only the first page. Witness, I'm going to now show the next document, which is 2D707. Could you please look at the document for us. This is another report. Have you located it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is another report which was signed by Toni Kolak. As it says here, he was the chief of the Service for the Healthcare of the Wounded, and he sent this report to you; and the report speaks about the negotiations regarding the transport and protection of the wounded and the frail during the war operations in the territories of Konjic, and the date is 9 of May. Just briefly, Mr. Bagaric, could you tell us something about the report, which is very precise? Could you please explain what kind of negotiations are discussed here?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: This is a very important document and a very important moment during the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims, Bosniaks in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is very closely tied with the previous report, which speaks of the 16th April or one day before. So if we remember, that coincided with the killing of Bosniak Muslims in Ahmic [as interpreted] and the Croats in Kostajnica. As a healthcare service, at the request and upon their implorations [as interpreted], because they were completely blocked in Konjic, we tried to talk to the International Red Cross and to organise the transport of all the wounded, i.e., those who needed further assistance. On several occasions, I believe on two occasions, we went down there to Jablanica in the organisation of the International Red Cross. However, the Muslim Bosniak authorities did not allow us passage and access to the wounded. We were not allowed access, and the International Red Cross was not allowed access. And then I asked Mr. Petkovic, present here in the courtroom, and asked him whether we could organise or talk to Mr. Morales, the respective of the Spanish Battalion of the UNPROFOR - I'm very grateful to him to this very day - I wanted to ask him for a meeting at a higher level in order to be able to organise a transport of our men. Owing to all who are present here today and Mr. Morales, the meeting was indeed organised. Mr. Morales organised the meeting with Mr. Halilovic, who was the commander of the BiH Army, and Mr. Petkovic, the commander of the Main Staff of the HVO. I and my colleagues, doctors, we were involved in the meeting, and the objective was to achieve the objective that I've spoken about. And I was at the meeting in Konjic, at the military base there. Mr. Morales also came to the meeting. He was the commander at an even higher UNPROFOR level, and we achieved a gentleman's agreement that made me really happy at the time and very proud also. I was happy because I believed that we would be able to help those who needed our help the most, and I was also very proud for our own participation, the participation of the HVO headed by Mr. Petkovic. Mr. Petkovic was very professional and he told them, in very professional terms, Let's see what the problem is and how we can remove the problem. Then there were accusations on the part of the Muslim side. They tried to accuse us of various obstructions, but they were the ones who were putting obstructions in our way, and everybody was clear on that, the representatives of the international community and everybody else. It was finally agreed that we would take three different digressions in order to transport our wounded and to enable the Bosnian Army to tour the points that were of some interest to them. So when we headed off to the field, I was personally in the column, i.e., I was Mr. Petkovic's escort, and we went to Sovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, can I please draw your attention to something. I would like to have a very clear transcript. It says here in the middle of the first page, as you said it yourself, "it was agreed that we should proceed in three directions," and those directions were Konjic, Zaslivlje, Zabrdje --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: -- Stari Grad, Ostrozac, Celebici, Klis, Kostajnica, Buscak, Trusina, Butorovic Polje, Obriverca [phoen], and Sovici and Doljani, and all the prisons there. The report is very precise, but I would like to ask you this: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you managed to visit and what you didn't manage to visit of all the things that you had planned to visit. And just for the transcript, I can notice that not all the places have been recorded properly, but later on I will dictate the names of the places that have not been recorded. Go on, sir.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic wanted us to go to Sovici because he had accused the HVO for the alleged crimes that had been committed there, and we insisted on going to the place where the crime did happen, and that was Trusina and the part between Sajnica [phoen] and Buscak, and so on and so forth; and the third direction was Zabrdje and Zaslivlje and so on and so forth. We managed to go to Sovici. We were in Sovici, and to my great satisfaction and to the satisfaction of everybody in the group, there had been no crimes committed against the civilians, and this was confirmed by the Muslims who were detained. And when we were there, there was nothing there. And as for the other two directions, we didn't take any of them because the BiH Army had blocked the convoy, the UNPROFOR convoy headed by Morales and forced him to return to Mostar. In other words, on our part, we returned without our business completed because we did not go to Zabrdje or Zaslivlje or Trusina or anywhere near there, although that was our main objective and that was the reason we had asked for the meeting in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that you didn't go to Zaslivlje. Can you repeat, for the purpose of the transcript, where you didn't go?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: We did not go to the other remaining directions, Zabrdje and Zaslivlje. That's that section and the other section is Kostajnica and these villages where the crimes actually took place, the one referred to in the previous report by my colleague, a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber at the time what was happening in Turija, Zaslivlje and Zabrdje, where you did go, where you wanted to go. Who was in that area? Did go in that area? Turija, Zabrdje and Zaslivlje.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: In that area, there were Croats who all stayed. Actually, they were in the Konjic enclave, but that was a separate enclave. They happened to be in a sandwich with Bosnian forces on one side and the Army of Republika Srpska on the other side, and I think that later they managed to get out through the Serbian side somehow.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you now please look at document 2D74 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Nozica. Witness, I would like to ask you a question of you. In the course of this last lengthy period of your answer, you have spoken of "our wounded, our wounded." Could you explain to the Chamber what you mean by "our wounded"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We had a report from these villages, Trusina, Sajonica [phoen], Kostajnica, that there were many wounded members of the HVO and civilians there, and because of them we asked this meeting to be organised in the first place. We didn't manage to get to them and bring them out. That's what it's about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Your answer, Mr. Bagaric, leads me to conclude that they were persons of Muslim ethnicity that you were concerned with here, the wounded that were members of the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in this specific case I used the term "our," and perhaps that confused you and you're, in a way, not understanding. In this case, the wounded were exclusively members of the Croatian Defence Council and Croats who were living there, civilians, so the wounded were all the people that we could reach and treat. But in this particular case, the wounded did also happen all to be Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I do not agree that I was confused, actually. I had supposed that this was the case, but I wanted to have it clear so that we are not doing guess-work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I have been warned correctly that on page 54, on line 22, the word "wounded" is missing when the witness was talking about that. He was talking about wounded members of the HVO and civilians. The word "wounded" is missing, and that is why it doesn't quite make sense. Anyway, that was the task of the mission the way the witness described it. Can we look at the next document, 2D745, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a report of the same date about the humanitarian convoy's trip to Klisa and Vrci? Is it the same trip? Mr. Tugomir Gveric, chief of the Medical headquarters of the HZ-HB is writing this report. Can you tell us what the difference is between the two reports?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: The only difference is the trip that the two doctors went to. The two of them, Kolak and Tugomir Gveric went in two different directions. I went in the third direction, in the third destination. We did manage to complete our assignments, both to the satisfaction of the Bosnian commanders and us, me as a doctor, but the other two trips we were not able to complete. We didn't manage to reach the destination. That is why they wrote two different reports, but essentially the reports cover the same events.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When we're talking about reports from the field, let us look at document 2D1296. That would be the next document. This is a document of the 9th of June, signed once again by the chief of the Medical Corps, Mr. Drago Dzambas, and he says in the first sentence of the first paragraph that Travnik fell. The second paragraph talks about the hospital in Nova Bila which is operating above its capacity and that 213 people were wounded over a period of five days. It talks about a shortage of oxygen, again about the evacuation in Split, and it talks about the drama happening in Travnik. It also talks about wounded doctors and that two doctors, Valjan and --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Valjan?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me, Valjan and Stipinov. Their outlook is uncertain. Can you please comment on this document, Mr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: This is one of the typical reports that was sent from the Nova Bila Hospital which I referred to earlier. This specifically refers to the events related to the expulsion of the Croatian civilian population from Travnik and the take-over of the whole town by the Bosniaks or by the Muslim Army. The report covers a difficult situation in a very small area, the overall situation, and especially in terms of the treatment of the wounded in the Nova Bila Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at the next document, 2D569. It's a report from the 3rd Brigade in Fojnica from the 2nd of July, referring to your order. It's being sent to the chief of the Medical Services, Drago Dzambas. The chief of the medical brigade of that brigade talks -- battalion talks about the number of wounded and the number of soldiers killed, as well as the number of civilians who were killed and wounded: 99 soldiers were wounded, 46 soldiers were killed. Can you tell us whether similar or this report reached you? It says, at the top of the document, that it was being sent to the Defence Department, to the Health Sector or Medical Sector.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, are these the reports that would also reach you from the field?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think this refers to the Fojnica situation, something similar to what previously happened in Travnik, so this is a Central Bosnian mixed population town with a majority Croatian population, where what happened happened, and we could see there was a large number of victims, a lot of suffering, and then Bosniak Muslims overran that whole area and the civilians had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now we have 2D00461. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The document is signed by Mr. Ivo Sandrk on the behalf of the HVO Medical Staff, and also the name of Mr. Siljeg is there. The date is the 22nd of July. What it says here is: "I'm addressing you maybe for the last time ..." And you can see who the letter is addressed to, the UN British Battalion, Major Bins, Captain Holden and it says: "I am addressing you maybe for the last time so that we can jointly try to do everything to save the lives of hundreds of wounded children, soldiers, and civilians from Bugojno. Already tomorrow, such help may not be needed." Can you tell us about that situation in Bugojno and can you comment on this document, please?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: For the third time, we are seeing the same kind of thing happening, in this case in Bugojno, because of a high concentration of Bosnia Muslim forces, people who were also expelled from other places in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as army members, people who were armed. The Croats in Bugojno got into a very difficult situation, and this is a very sad story of Bugojno which actually did -- was completely cleansed of Croats. Unfortunately, the crimes that took place there were never punished, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, we saw the situation previously in Travnik. Then we saw the situation in Fojnica, and now we're seeing the situation in Bugojno. I know what you are trying to say, but I think for the purposes of the transcript and the Trial Chamber, it would be good for you to say explicitly who occupied those places and who expelled the Croats from those towns.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, this was a time of the full escalation of the conflict between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council, and these towns were all entirely captured by the armija, the Bosnian Muslim side; and those who were expelled from all three of these towns were exclusively or in the majority of cases Croats who, unfortunately, specifically in Bugojno, made up 40 percent of the population; maybe not 40 percent, but the ratio between Croats and Muslims was more or less equal. And then the Croatian population was completely expelled. And despite all efforts at this moment, I think right now there is 6.000 or 7.000 -- a population of 6.000 or 7.000 Croats there, compared to the previous figure of 30.000 before the war, which I think is still quite a considerable success in getting those people to come back, these Croats who are there now who managed to return. At one point in time, practically all of the Croats were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, from this previous document, which is an exhibit and seen before in the courtroom, which actually is a request for help in the evacuation of the wounded, can we now please look at the next document? This is 2D465. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This was signed by Mr. Sandrk, and the document is being sent to you. It also focuses on the need to evacuate the wounded; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. It refers to all the wounded, because there was a hospital there where both Bosnian Muslims and Croats were being treated up until the time of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 2 of this document where this actually is stated: "I have just arrived from the Bugojno War Hospital in the presence of the UNPROFOR and the observers. An agreement was reached to evacuate the same. All wounded members of the HVO and wounded civilians are going to be evacuated to Gornji Vakuf." Already he is talking about the beginning of this evacuation; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at document 2D467 on the same topic. This document was also signed by the chief of the HVO SIK, Dr. Ivo Sandrk, and the document talks about the evacuation of the wounded from the HVO hospital in Bugojno according to the days. Mr. Bagaric, can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at document 2D726. 2D726.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I have to take a different binder now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Go ahead. Very well. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, this is sent from Busovaca. The documents are arranged in chronological order. This is a report of the 1st of August, 1993 from the chief of the medical corps of the Nikola Subic Zrinski Brigade, sending information about persons killed and wounded, both civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you look at the next document. This is 2D728. It's a report of the 4th of August, from the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade in Novi Travnik, from the 4th of August we said, and it mentions the number of killed soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It also says that two members of the brigade were killed by the Serbian aggressor. The next document is more or less the same. That is 2D729. Mr. Bagaric, this is also a report of the Vitez Brigade service, the chief of the Medical Corps. He's sending a report on the number of persons killed and wounded, and the report is dated the 5th of August, 1993. You received reports like this one, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, reports like this, or similar ones, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next document would be 2D00730. It's a little bit different. It's a request for the transport of wounded by a helicopter. It's signed by Mr. Dzambas. It's a request for evacuation from the military hospital in Bila. Mr. Bagaric, we did talk about the military hospital. Can you tell us briefly about the number of requests for evacuations that were carried out?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, we can see numerous requests here, but I know that these requests occurred on a daily basis, almost, and they indicate actually the gravity of the situation that we were in, especially the Croats of Central Bosnia; in Nova Bila in this instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now to look at -- Mr. Bagaric, perhaps it would seem excessive, but was there a different way of evacuating these people, other than by helicopter?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Well, it's generally known that the transport links with Central Bosnia were severed because of the conflict between the armija and the HVO; so I, as the chief of the Medical Corps, or the commander, rather, of the Medical Corps of the HVO, was very concerned to receive requests like this every day for assistance, for help, for evacuation, to do this or that, but we exclusively depended on helicopter flights, which had to be approved by UNPROFOR, and this is why we had to send them out to UNPROFOR and to the commanders -- or receive them also from commanders and were sending them on to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bagaric, let's look at another report now. This is 2D712. It's a list, actually, of those wounded and killed. This is a list. It says "The Defence Department, the Healthcare Sector." I would kindly ask you to tell us this: Were these lists made based on the previous lists and reports?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: With a remark that we also have the names of the persons who were wounded and killed here. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber, how were these lists compiled?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: What I find unusual in the document is the fact that I can see the date here, the 1st of August, 1993, and down there is -- there are different dates; the 2nd, the 4th, the 5th of August. So I don't know -- I don't understand how this happened. Does this mean that the top date is erroneous or not? I am a bit confused.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, I'm asking an explanation from you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That question is asked and answered. The witness says he doesn't understand. I don't understand either, Ms. Nozica, what we are to do with all this, these numbers of wounded. I frankly do not see the pertinent or relevance of these documents to our case. Perhaps you can clarify. They're also rather repetitious, as we have had that before.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm asking the witness about what he did in the sector, and the witness told us what the sector did. The Health Sector did receive reports from the field. They forwarded those reports, and I'm asking the witness exactly what you have just said. The witness said that he's confused, and I'm asking the witness whether he can explain the source of confusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It says here "the Health Sector." Maybe the witness can tell us whether this was, indeed, done in the Healthcare Sector. If he think it wasn't, then I'll skip this document.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Can you please bear with me. Your Honours, I am not doubting the accuracy of the data, which means that on the 1st of August, a certain number of people were wounded, and then some others on the 2nd of August. I believe that this is correct. However, I am puzzled by the date up there. I believe that we probably had collected the data, our service did it, and then our service compiled a summary report, and I believe that the previous date was retained by mistake. It's really confusing, I must say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, which service was in charge of compiling the data? You're saying "the service." Which service was that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I said that within our Medical Staff, we had a department or a service -- I don't know how to call it. For a while it was "department" and then it was a service, the Information and Documentation Service it was called, and that service collected information from the field in order to be able to inform anybody about the situation or document the situation in the field. In other words, this served for us to be able to monitor the overall situation with the healthcare in the territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at the following document, 2D503. This is a document which was compiled in a similar way. Again, it was headed by the Healthcare centre, but the date is different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to put a question with regard to the previous document. Dr. Bagaric, I don't know if you know, but I assume you do, are all these people reported here Croats on the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly not. I did not check. I can do it, if you wish me to, I can even speculate, but I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can you tell us how the names were found? Who set up the list originally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we had communication with our doctors in the field, and they were the first source of information because they were in immediate contact with anybody who was wounded or they learned about anybody who had been killed, they maintained records which they forwarded to us. So it went from one doctor to another. I assume -- or, rather, I don't assume, I know it for a fact that doctors also submitted information to their respective commanders in their own units. For example, here it would be the brigades or the military districts, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There is a section entitled -- subsection "Soldiers killed." Would that include soldiers of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose -- or, rather, I'm convinced that this is not the case. The chiefs of the medical services in the HVO units were the ones that followed the HVO units, and this concerns primarily HVO members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Right, thank you. That's quite convincing also. And there are two civilians, Nametak and Kresic. To me, by now, it sounds rather like Croatian than Muslim names, but you know much better than I do, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Which page is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Dead civilians, yes. Kresic, Marina, I assume she's Croat. And as for Mija Nametak, I'm not quite sure. I can't be sure. I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I believe that what I'm going to say is very important, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Go on, then.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: It says here on the 7th of August, 1993, or the 6th of August, 1993, we have here Croats, if this is what we are going to be looking at, we have Croats and also Muslim Bosniaks, and we also have their diagnosis. This points to the fact that only the doctors could compile the reports of this kind, because who else could have been able to determine the diagnosis or the diagnostic situation after the wounding? And I believe that this was important, and I apologise for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: To follow up on His Honour Trechsel's question, let's look at the page where it says "Mirko Golemac", and then on the 2nd of August, it says: "Senad Saric," 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9, are you following me, 10, 11, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19. Would all these be Bosniak names?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, yes. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, when it comes to the wounded, were those people treated at the HVO hospitals, regardless of their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely, regardless of their ethnic background or their affiliation to a unit. They all enjoy the same treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a brief comment about the following document, 2D503. Is that the same kind of report?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bagaric, can we look at 2D761.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a report on the negotiations with the Muslim side regarding the evacuation of the wounded in Medjugorje, and the date is 1st September through 6 September?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It says in the first sentence that: "At 1000 hours on 1 September 1993, in the Spanish Battalion base in Medjugorje, negotiations started about the implementation of the agreement on the evacuation of the seriously sick and wounded persons from Nova Bila and Mostar ..."

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And at the Sarajevo Airport. This was signed on the 1st of August, 1993, General Petkovic, Delic, and this was testified to by Mr. Briquemont. Do you know anything about this meeting, Mr. Bagaric?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: It was a long time ago, but I am convinced that I personally attended that meeting in Sarajevo, if this was signed in Sarajevo. I apologise. Does it say anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: The meeting took place before the date that is indicated here as the 7th of September. I was personally present at the meeting, because Mr. Petkovic had invited me to attend as the chief of the Medical Service of the HVO, to visit Sarajevo to attend the meeting. That was at the time when Sarajevo was fully encircled. And I had an occasion to ask Mr. Delic to organise something, and this is how I remember the meeting. I remember it for the wounded and for what I was asked by Mr. Delic to do; and that is to organise a meeting between the head of the Medical Service of the BH Army and me personally, because I thought if we were to establish good communication, then our wounded, irrespective of their affiliation, would enjoy a much better chance for healthcare, for transport, and all the other benefits. However, I remember that Mr. Delic was not interested in that kind of meeting. I pursued those attempts a lot of times. I talked to the international community, UNPROFOR, asking them to mediate between us and the other side in order to arrange such a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bagaric. This is going to be my next set of questions, but let's look at two more things in this document. On the second page, in the Croatian version, which is also page 4 in the English version - in Croatian, this is page 2, paragraph 3 - the document was signed by the Control and Inspection, Mr. Stevo Sarlik [phoen]. I believe I've forgotten to say that. It says here: "I went to Mostar to be present with UNPROFOR when MOS wounded were taken on board." I would like to emphasise that previously you can see that the date is the 3rd of September?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And it says what ensued was a MOS mortar attack on the part of town under the control of the HVO. Eighteen civilians were wounded, five of them children, and five civilians were killed. Among the wounded civilians, there were eight Muslims. It is clear that the aim of the attack was for the MOS to show the public that the evacuation could not be carried out for security reasons. Mr. Bagaric, two questions. First of all, do you remember this event at all?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Second question: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, how often did such attacks happen while you were working in Mostar? I believe you had an office in Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did spend a lot of time in Mostar throughout my engagement, and such attacks were frequent. This is one which resulted in the wounding and killing of civilians and children. I personally witnessed frequent mortar and all other attacks on MOS. However, to be honest, it was very hard for me to tell the difference. I didn't know whether the fire came from the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska or from the Muslim Bosniak positions, but the truth is that the town did come under shell attacks every now and then. But I believe that it would be very important for the Trial Chamber to know and to bear in mind that this document clearly shows that my colleague, Mr. Sandrk, who was chief of our Control and Inspection Service, he noted the lack of interest on the part of the Muslim Bosniak side and the evacuation of the wounded. And it really is very hard to understand the whole thing because the patients and the Muslim doctors in the east part of Mostar during the conflict with the Croats and the HVO were indeed in very dire straits, their situation was very difficult. However, we had a similar if not the same or even a worse situation in Bila, and we had agreed upon an evacuation exercise for all, everybody for everybody. However, you could sense that the Muslim Bosniak side was hesitating, dragging their feet, and I didn't know why. I was never clear on the reason why they would do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You are probably talking about the part of the document which starts on the same page and says: "On the 5th of September, 1993," this is page 5, paragraph 2 in the English version. Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going to have to show you another list. The document number is 2D508, and it speaks about the same incident. And on the penultimate page of this document, you confirmed that you know about a mortar shell that had fallen and that some people were killed and wounded. And now look at the date the 3rd of September, where it says: "The wounded." Why do you remember this event, Mr. Bagaric? What makes it so striking to you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Because children were killed, children died.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now let's go to the penultimate page. You see a list of 17 persons, civilians, and could you please look at the diagnosis. And as a doctor, I don't want you to speculate, can you tell us whether those people were wounded? Look at the diagnosis and tell us whether it is possible that they were wounded in the way it is described in the previous document, by mortar fire.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: What page is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It is 2D508, penultimate page. The date is 3rd of September. Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Penultimate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: 3rd of September. It starts with "Maric, Marijana." Could you please tell us, look at the diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is precisely that. I really can't tell you exactly because I can't remember the names of the children who were killed, but it is obvious that all of these were wounds inflicted by explosions and resulted in explosive trauma. As you can see here, due to explosion, these individuals suffered wounds to their heads, chest, stomach, shoulders, again chest cavity.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now, again, could you please briefly comment upon the names that you see in front of you. Just take a glance and tell us whether there are Croats and Muslims here.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes, both.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now the last entry, the civilians who were killed on the 3rd of September.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And also can you please confirm that we see here five names of both Croats and Bosniak Muslims?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, so far you have mentioned having had good communication with international organisations. I'm going to ask you to explain to the Trial Chamber which international organisations you communicated with in the course of this period from September 1992 up to sometime -- let's say the Washington Accords. Which were the international organisations that you communicated with, how -- is there anything you would like to add about their behaviour, your contacts with them, or any such thing?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were practically constantly in communication with the UN, the UNHCR, and the International Red Cross, and the Doctors Without Borders, as much as we could. It's my impression -- and actually I would very much like to be allowed to be given the time to say what I mean to say on this topic and for that to be recorded in the transcript. My experience from that conflict or from that period of the war is that the international organisations, either due to objective reasons or often subjective reasons, did not and were not able to do much about the conflict. Simply, in terms of what I talked about, often one would monitor if the sides in the conflict were in accord, if one or the other side was accepting something or not. The interventions would be delayed or postponed, and I think that in terms of that, the doctors who were together with me in that area believe that the experiences that we had there, generally we - I am thinking of doctors of Croat and of Bosnian Muslim ethnicity - should provide an input in cases of future conflicts. For example, we proposed for a joint hospital to be formed in Mostar and that our existing HVO war hospital be used both for the Croats and for Bosnian Muslims and members of their army, but I know that two members of the UN and international organisations seemed to be an impossible mission. But I'm convinced that everything is possible if you wish to carry through and if there is at least one side that is in accord, and evidence of that is that throughout that whole period in Mostar, we worked on the actual front-line, that the hospital in Mostar was on the actual front-line; so, therefore, this is one issue, not to mention other matters that had to do with refugee camps, prisoners, rather in which way this humanitarian activity could be advanced. Perhaps had Ovcara and Vukovar been prevented, Srebrenica might not have happened. Once Srebrenica did happen, then, as an international institution, we have the case of Rwanda. So my professor of public health, my colleague who participated in these events in Mostar, Professor Slobodan [indiscernible], wrote and published a very important article in which he proposes 12 elements in order to improve things on the basis of experiences during the war, the improving of humanitarian law and other aspects that had to do with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I didn't interrupt you, Mr. Bagaric.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now I would like to go back to your contacts with international organisations. I'm going to put a general question to you, and then we're going to move to documents that show that. You said you had contacts with different international organisations?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How, objectively, did they contribute to the resolution of health issues in that area? What are your experiences about that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Very often, the internation humanitarian organisations managed to help us, and of course any assistance was very welcome, but often what I talked about and what I'm very dissatisfied about would also happen. For example, we would be asking for medicines. I remember an officer from the World Health Organisation who said, We don't have medicines. Well, who is supposed to have them if the World Health Organisation doesn't have them. The International Red Cross, despite all the efforts -- well, let's say I remember a time when he told us that he could not help us in the transfer of doctors from one town, where there were plenty of them to another one where there was a total shortage because that would be counter to their mission. That was incomprehensible to me. Then these examples that I referred to; for example in the hospital, global hospital and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, let's look at a few documents that discuss that and some of your correspondence. The first one is 3D217 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, but we do have a number of important topics, so can you just comment on this request. Tell us to whom it's addressed and what it's about. 2D317.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, in the transcript, it says "3D217," but actually it's 317. Give us your comments.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: This is a document that speaks about us securing support and the treatment of our sick children, children who are from different areas of Herzegovina, who suffer from different illnesses. And now that we're looking at it, I can also see that these children are from different ethnic groups. This is one of the projects that was successfully implemented, where others did invest efforts in order to help us.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. This is something that is evident. I would like to emphasise that, that you say "our sick children." And we're talking about the 14th of April, 1993, and there is a list of 13, 14, 15. And then on the other side, where you signed it, we have the names. And so judging by the names, what would you say? Are we talking about Croats or Bosniaks here?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: What you said are Muslim children, the names you referred to, but of course there are Croats among them, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, I'm now going to ask you to comment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to stop you. It's 20 to 6.00, so 20 minutes' break, and we will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're now in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, I was told that I still have an hour and 38 minutes for my examination-in-chief, and since we still have at least two or three large topics that we have to cover, I'm just going to ask you for a brief comment on the documents that I'm going to show you, and perhaps the last one we will look at in more detail. Can you please look at the following document. This is your communication with international organisations. Could you please look at 2D706. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is the 28th of April. You are sending the letter to the International Red Cross, and you are referring to the situation in Konjic. Does that have to do with the situation that you referred to earlier in the time-period that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Can you please look at the next document. This is 2D710, 2D710, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry for being meticulous, Ms. Nozica. The previous document, you indicated that the date was 25th of April, and all I see is "the 5th of May." So probably I did something wrong, and I stand to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document 2D706, 2D706.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I was with the next document, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at document 2D710. I think that is the document that I asked for, 2D710. Have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: You are skipping one document? I'm talking about 2D519.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we will go back to 519, but can you please comment on 2D710?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you comment on this document?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: This refers to the situation that I talked about in Bugojno, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And here you're addressing the UN; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Let us go back now to document 2D519.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what the document is about?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: This is the situation in Konjic, when we tried to enter all of those places together with the UN in Konjic and when we failed. I'm actually again addressing the UN and attaching my reports from the field, and they, themselves, also know that that's how it was. And I'm just saying that we did not succeed in completing our task.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, can we look at 2D521.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is being sent to the Spanish Battalion. You are writing to them on the 31st of July, and you're saying that at 7.00, there were ambushes in Kucani and Toscenica when the Muslims ambushed and killed ambulance driver, Ivan Topic and medical technician, Zvonko Tolj. At that time, they took the driver in an unknown direction as well as medical technicians. Do you remember the situation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Herve Kalubaric [phoen] I know personally. This is correct information, and unfortunately the event did take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The next document is 2D713. This is your address to the International Red Cross of the 2nd of August?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is connected to the previous event, and we are asking them to establish a connection with these people. And I remember that they did that, they communicated with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, 2D716. In the original document, I can see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I am concerned whether these were captured, and I want to know whether they were released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After a couple of months, they were freed, but it was after a couple of months. I don't know exactly how long it took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you look at document 2D716, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This document is of the 23rd of September and again talks about the situation in Central Bosnia. Again, it talks about the transport of sick and wounded persons from Nova Bila. I'm just asking you if this is one of the requests you sent to international organisations for the transport of wounded from the hospitals that were referred to.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, and it confirms that the situation in Central Bosnia was constantly difficult at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we now skip a document, and if you can look at 2D460 now. We can speed things up a little bit. This is a document of the 16th of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, again the story is repeated, an unresolved situation where we are persistently trying to establish communication and save the wounded up there, and the sick.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at document 2D733 now. This is again the 16th of January, 1994. The UN Observers and the UNPROFOR Command are being addressed. Can you please look at page 1, and if you can just comment what you suggest here.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Isn't this the same paper? I think that it is.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think this is the -- only the translation of this paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, what is your suggestion about this document here?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: We are suggesting that the routes of evacuation, manner of transport of the wounded, members of the HVO and civilians, are done in a way that it's carried out either by UNPROFOR or that they are escorted by UNPROFOR or taken out by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, excuse me, please, but can you please look at the screen. I'm talking about document 2D733. You can see it on your monitor, 733. This is your request to the UN observers and the UNPROFOR Command in Kiseljak, and you say: "In view of the fact that the situation regarding help for the wounded is getting worse in Bosnia and Herzegovina," and you're talking about saving lives, and you're asking that commanders of Health Services of the HVO and the B and H Army meet in order that they could agree, in the presence of members of the Observer mission?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: This is one of our frequent requests aimed at bringing together the leaders in the Medical Service, because we believed if this happened the situation in the field would be alleviated and contribute to a cessation of combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, just so that all of this is clear, we're talking about bringing together commanders of the HVO and B and H Army health services? Is that being interpreted correctly on my part, you were talking about bringing them together?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, let us finally look at a document that summarises what we're talking about. This is document 2D512 [as interpreted]. It's a memo of yours of the 20th of December, 1993, talking about the situation with the wounded, the sick, the supply of medicines and equipment, and the relations between the Muslim and Croat side, the HVO and the ABiH. It's sent to the UNPROFOR, UNHCR, and the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Ms. Nozica, I think the number is 502 and not 512.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Yes, I have just been told that the transcript is incorrect. It's 2D502. I was not paying attention to the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: This is a very important document. In a certain way, it provides a lot of details, talking about the problem and issue of our sick and wounded, and in more general terms about the situation on the ground; and that is why this document, I'm asking the other side and the representatives of international institutions to assist us, to help us in establishing contact with the other side, with a view to transporting our wounded and sick and providing them full medical assistance. And I'm talking about both Croats and Muslims, without any conditions. In one place here, I am saying that should we not be able to agree definitely, then the Bosniak Muslim side should take their patients wherever they want to take them. If they cannot be treated in the eastern side of Mostar, then they should either bring their patients to the western part of Mostar or take them to Sarajevo. I apologise. Sarajevo would have been very hard because Sarajevo was under very grave circumstances. However, very often they had to take people to Turkey and other countries of the European Union that were willing to assist their sick and wounded. That's why we are asking them to enable that to happen. I'm talking about the wounded, about the sick, about medical institutions and medical equipment, about medical supplies, and so on and so forth. This is a document which was issued at the end of the year 1993. Before the end of the war, a lot of time elapsed, and if we had been able to reach an agreement at that time, I'm sure that many, many people, our patients, Muslims, Croats, would have survived the terrible and unnecessary conflict. And I'm very sincere when I say that all those were victims of the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina that were not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, according to your proposal that was sent to all the relevant addressees of the international community, you are dividing sick people into two categories, and your proposal is that all the sick and wounded could be treated, irrespective of differences among people, irrespective of the fact whether they were ones or the others, and that all available institutions should be used. And under C, you're saying that with the help of international institutions, "we should improve the situation in the existing institutions in Bosnia-Herzegovina," and under C used the health institution in Croatia which was agreed with the minister of health in the Republic of Croatia. Could you please tell us whether the wounded members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina also went to Croatia after having been evacuated from the territory of East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, not only from the territory of East Mostar, but also all the war-struck areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, thousands upon thousands of patients, wounded soldiers, civilians, Muslims, but there were also Serbs -- more Muslims than Serbs, but there were Serbs as well. There were also thousands of Croats who were treated and taken care of in Croatian hospitals, without any questions asked, without any money; and this to my mind was the biggest humanitarian aid that one state extended to another during a conflict, during the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I believe there was no single state that helped Bosnia and Herzegovina to that extent. I don't know of any historical case that would be comparable. And the wounded are just one part of the story, and sick. There was a lot more humanitarian aid which arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina and reached both Muslims and Croats from Croatia and via Croatia by land or by sea, and it's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm now going to draw your attention to the part in which you're talking about drugs and medicines, but before that, I would like to ask you this: Were there any reactions to this letter of yours? Did anybody inform you that steps could be taken?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: The most frustrating thing for a man who was trying to deal with a problem in the war was the fact that very often there was no reply whatsoever, none. I assume that the representatives of the international community did send that to the other side and they did not accept this gesture, because if they had done that, they would not have been able to enjoy the reputation of a victim, to put it that way. I don't have any other explanation. And when I requested from the international community representatives to tell me what was going on and what could be done, they would always tell me, We are waiting for their reply. And we were always waiting and waiting and waiting, until the end of the war, and it was not forthcoming, it never arrived; only every now and then there were meetings organised, and then with the assistance of generals and commanders, some agreements would be signed about the transport of one person or the other. But this was all in the hands of the other side, which was dragging their feet and procrastinating, and I don't know why to this very day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to link up this last answer with a question I meant to ask, because since the beginning of the afternoon I've been carefully looking at all the documents and I have the feeling or even the certainty, reading the report you drafted, among other things, paragraph F in Chapter 1, that somehow you are challenging the international institutions who seem to have taken a stand in favour of the opponent, and the fact that you said that you sent a letter and got no reply. This is what one can infer from this. Is this what you experienced in the field, because you're mentioning examples to the effect that the international organisations established institutions in Tuzla, Zenica, et cetera, Muslim areas, and apparently nothing in Croatian zones. Now, my question is as follows: Were your reports based on subjective impressions or was this actually what was happening in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honours, certainly that I am telling you about my impressions. It is inevitable. I had regular communication with representatives of the international community and other institutions. However, this report, i.e., this request, was based primarily on the data that we had received from the field. Let me remind you, Central Bosnia was encircled, fully encircled, the hospital in Bila, the hospital in Zepce, the hospital up there in Orasje, and so on and so forth, and now if we compare our requests that we sent to the international institutions and their response then, I would say that all the time we had a feeling that as a matter of fact, their responses did not match our requests. Their reactions were not sufficient. Of course, they helped us. Of course, they assisted us. From time to time, they played the key role, which I have emphasised here in paragraph F. I'm saying here that -- just a moment. Bear with me, please. Let me not waste your time. I'm sure it's there. I often did this. I thanked the international institutions for everything that they did, but it always seemed to me that there was much room left to do more and that the support was not forthcoming, not to the extend we would have wanted. There were cases, and I'm aware of such cases, when, for example, a field hospital was built and used by Muslim Bosniaks in Bosnia, and nothing of the kind was ever built in Bila, where the hospital was actually in the church. When we asked for some wounded to be transported, as a rule this would be delayed ad nauseam. I know that representatives of the international community were limited by the willingness of the Bosnian Muslim side. I know that. I'm aware of that. However, I was bothered by the lack of effectiveness and efficiency. At least, that's how it looked like from my point of view.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the Trial Chamber and Their Honours, and now I would like us to look at the part entitled "Medical Supplies" on the second page of this document, just one part that will be our introduction for our next topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You are saying in the document: "Throughout the war, we have tried to supply all medical institutions with additional medicines and drugs, irrespective of who the institutions belonged to and who they were treating. Whenever the Muslim side requested medicines from us, they would receive them on the same day. Enclosed please find some of the dispatch notes for such drugs." Mr. Bagaric, the next topic that I would like to ask you about are the relationships with the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Here, you are stating one thing, and let me ask you this first: What was your relationship with the healthcare of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina before the conflict? And then we'll go back to the topic of that relationship during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: With the leave of the Trial Chamber, I would like to comment on Article F in my letter, because I believe that I still owe you the explanation. I'm saying here that the engagement is valued, because any support to the other side is good; however, it seems to us that we lack that support or do not receive it to the same extent. I accept, Your Honours, that I may have been subjective in all that. However, I'm absolutely convinced that the international institutions could work towards improving their efficiency and effectiveness, and this is something that leaves a lot to be desired. And as for your question, Madam Nozica, our cooperation with the other side and our colleagues on the other side before the conflict with the Muslims, between the Croats and Muslims, was fair, if not excellent. We established our war hospitals together. We cooperated, we worked together, we treated people together, and that's how it was until the end of the war. However, my dissatisfaction arises from the part that concerns the areas under encirclement, for example, Croats in Central Bosnia in this case, and at the same time this was happening to the Muslims in the eastern side of Mostar. It seems that there was no support, that there was no cooperation between the doctors; and my impression is that this was not down to the doctors in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it was down to the commanders, who wouldn't let them do anything. To put it simply, they just did not allow this sort of open communication and cooperation between the two sides, between the medical personnel of the two sides. At the same time, the international institutions were trapped by their non-acceptance, and they did not know how to respond to that. I'm not saying that anybody was malicious or malevolent in the institutions of the international community, I'm not saying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: After the conflict with the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you were talking about what was happening before the conflict, and now after the conflict with the BiH Army did you continue seeking cooperation and offering solutions that would be mutually beneficial?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Of course, absolutely. I claim with full responsibility that we were doing that all the time. And, I repeat, it was a frustrating battle, because we never received, or at least not to the extent that we expected, the answers from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm sorry that I have to remind you of the time, but now we have arrived at a topic that is very important, and that's why I'm going to show I was series of documents talking about that. First of all, could you please look at 2D705.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You signed this document. This document has already been admitted. The date is 21st of December, 1992. And just briefly, I would kindly ask you to comment on your proposal put forth in this document. What was your idea?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: This was at a time when we still believed that Croats and Muslim Bosniaks would never come into conflict. However, we were afraid because there was already some skirmishes in the field. I was asking Mile Akmadzic, the prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to get in touch with my colleague in the BiH Army, and I wanted the two of us to appear together, based on the letter that was to ensue. I wanted us to appear together and to share -- to demonstrate how Croat and Muslim Bosniak doctors were against any conflict, that they wanted to prevent any possible war. That's one of the documents that I sent via the prime minister of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please look at the following document, dealing with the same topic, and then I will ask you whether there was any response to that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: I can comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you comment on the second document? First I have to call it, sir. This is 3D708. Could you please comment on that document very briefly, 3D708.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Here I am addressing actually the first letter. It's the enclosure of the second, more important document, I would say, and the second document was sent directly to the head of the Medical Service of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to their chief surgeon; and I am asking him to word a text the way he thinks it should be formed, any way he wanted, and I would co-sign it, and then we would return it to Mr. Robert Simon, who was the representative of the International Medical Corps. I have to apologise to everybody from the international community for my disaffection, because this Mr. Simon was really eager. He wanted to prevent any conflict, and he was a doctor, and he tried to convince me that if the doctors were to put forth such a position, that that possible -- that conflict could be prevented, and I still believe that this was possible. If the doctors were united and appeared together, if they didn't want a war and if they educated people in that sense, and especially based on the very grave experiences that we had suffered, then I believe that the conflict could have been prevented. This is a special part of the public health, as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we now look -- before that, I believe that the question is superfluous, but still I want to ask you. Did you receive any answers to your first or second letters?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, no answers whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you look at document 2D737.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I intervene to ask you the following question: Let's say that while looking at these two last documents, I'm very surprised, because you are in a hierarchal chain, and you write to the president of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina directly, and you write to your corresponding number who is in the opposite camp. So is this a habit in your country, where the rules of hierarchy are not respected, that is to say that you may write only with the permission of your chiefs, or does everybody do anything they want?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour, if you formed the wrong impression. Actually, 1992, the 21st of December, 1992, is the year of the conflict, the year of the war, so it's not a regular situation and, as such, sometimes calls for intervention which, in an ordered world, an ordered organisation, might seem irregular. But thanks to my acquaintance with Mr. Akmadzic, because I was a deputy in the Parliament, I believe that this was simply a gesture of goodwill, an attempt to communicate in a way that would not inflict harm on anyone, but that could produce certain positive results. On the other hand, I did consult my superiors, and nobody was opposed to me doing this. This is what it comes down to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you please look at the next document, 2D737, please. We simply arranged the documents chronologically to show this cooperation in terms of the medical work and medical equipment. This is the Trauma and Orthopaedic Service of the Dzemal Bijedic Medical Centre, and it's addressed on the 31st of December, 1992. Mr. Stojic was not there at the time. This was a request for certain instruments, technical aids, bandages, disinfectant, and other things for the hospital. And can you please tell us if you agree or not that assistance of this kind was being sent to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the area of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is Mr. Stojic's signature, stating that he approved this. I'm repeating again that we're talking about 1992, when there was no conflict between the Croats and the Bosnian Muslims. And it indicates that the Muslims were not in an easy situation, either. They were suffering from shortages, too, and required help, which I believe did arrive, because I think somebody did deliver this. I'm not familiar with this document. I haven't seen it, I didn't see it during the war or anything like that, but I do believe that the request was fulfilled, because it's initialled as being approved. So this is just part of our regular communication among doctors.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you look at the following document, 2D704. This is a list of essential medicines and material from the Medical Centre in Visoko of the 5th of December. There is no heading to whom the document is addressed. That's why I'm asking you. These are medicines. Do you remember? Do you remember whether it is stated to whom this request for medicines and equipment was addressed to and whether it was delivered?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Once again, I apologise, but this is a document of which I saw many during the war before the conflict between us broke out, so this is a request addressed to the Medical Service, our medical service, and perhaps it was sent to the Republic of Croatia. But they did that through us, so most often it would be the Split Hospital, which was actually the closest. It was on the road from Bosnia to Croatia. So therefore -- but I don't know really whether this was implemented in a way or not. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bagaric, I don't expect you to know everything about each before case, but on the basis of the documents that we saw, I'm going to ask you if you have information whether actions like this were carried out and medicines were delivered, and medical equipment, for the needs of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Army at this time.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you look at document 2D316. This is a notice. Let me just put a question. First, this is a result of a meeting on April 14th, 1993, and it's addressed to the Wartime Studio of Mostar. Can you please tell us what you know about this notice and the reaction to it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is April the 14th, 1993, already indicating a time indicating the possible of an open conflict, a war, a conflict between us Croats and Bosniak Muslims, on the radio that you referred to. In a very unprofessional, biased way, the hospital in Mostar was presented in the sense that Croats were not allowing this or that, and then I -- I was not the commander of the hospital, but because of these reasons, I organised this meeting, together with the hospital director and all the leading doctors, where, in a certain way, we expressed -- or actually rejected notice like this one and said that we needed to work together and that we were appealing to everyone that we should work together, and in that way we were actually contributing to what actually I was talking about the whole time here and what I was saying the whole time then. And I apologise, there's a sentence here which is -- well, I don't know if I would write it now, but at that time it was quite logical. Actually, it says: "On behalf of the Command and the doctors of the war hospital, support is being given in the war of the Croats and Muslims against the common enemy." Because at that time the Croats and the Muslims thought of the Serbs exclusively as the enemy, as their opponents, and also the wish was expressed that the conflicts, which are unnatural, should stop. And I know that perhaps it might seem a bit too much from me to the Trial Chamber, but I did believe in the dream that we could really contribute to the prevention of the conflict and the war, at least from the extent to which it occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look at document 2D318. It's an announcement of the 23rd of April, and it indicates the presence of the chief of the Medical Corps of the 4th Corps. Is this is another one of your attempts for a joint --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BAGARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I went to him and asked him to draft or set up a conversation, a talk, and to publicise everything that we wrote down here. I think that this meeting was held at the Command of the army.
